The language accepted by a DFA is the set of all input strings over its alphabet that lead the automaton to an accepting state when processed.

A string of length zero, denoted by ε, containing no elements.
A subset of the set of all strings (Σ*) over an alphabet Σ, representing a collection of strings recognized or defined by an automaton.
Theory involving the classification of computational problems that are both in NP and as hard as any problem in NP.

A language that contains no strings; symbolically ∅.

A finite ordered sequence of elements from a given alphabet.

Claim 1.6. Consider the DFA M3, and for each state q let Lq be the set of strings x ∈{a, b}∗that make the
DFA reach from q0 to q. Then we have
Lq0 = {ε},
Lq1 = {awa | w ∈{a, b}∗} ∪{a},
Lq2 = {awb | w ∈{a, b}∗}
Lr1 = {bwb | w ∈{a, b}∗} ∪{b},
Lr2 = {bwa | w ∈{a, b}∗}.
Proof. Let x ∈{a, b}∗and denote by n the length of x. We prove by induction on n the set Lq to which x
belongs. For n = 0 we only have the string x = ε, and it is clear that x ∈Lq0. For n = 1, we have x = a
that is clearly in Lq1, and x = b that is clearly in Lr1.
We now move on to the inductive step. Let n ⩾1; we assume that the statement is true for all strings
of length at most n, and prove it for x of length |x| = n + 1. As n + 1 ⩾2 we may write x = σwτ where
σ, τ ∈{a, b}and w ∈{a, b}∗. We now do case analysis according to σ and τ:
1. Consider the string σw, which has length n. Suppose first that σ = a. Then, by the induction
hypothesis, if w ends in a or w = ∅then M(σw) reaches q1, and otherwise M(σw) reaches q2. Thus,
by the transition table of M2, if τ = a then M(σwτ) reaches q1 so x ∈Lq1, and if τ = b, then
M(σwτ) reaches q2 so x ∈Lq2.
Next, suppose that σ = b. By the induction hypothesis, if w ends in a b or w = ∅then M(σw) reaches
r1, and otherwise M(σw) reaches r2. Thus, by the transition table of M2, if τ = b then M(σwτ)
reaches r1 so x ∈Lr1, and if τ = a, then M(σwτ) reaches r2 so x ∈Lr2.
So far we have seen examples of DFAs and seen some ways of arguing about what language they accept.
In the recitation and problem set, you will see a few more such examples.

6.14 Automata, Computability and Complexity Theory
Lecture 1
Dor Minzer
Our main goal in this course is to introduce a mathematical formalism of the notion of computation and
ways of arguing about it. In particular, we will give meaning to statements along the lines of “problem X
is computable”, and formalize various notions of efficiency that you may have seen in previous courses.
Roughly speaking, the course will consist of 3 parts:
1. Automata theory: In the first part of the course we will introduce the most basic computational model,
known as Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA), and study the class of problems that it can compute,
which are known as regular languages.
This part of the course will help to warm up to the formalistic/proof based approach that this course
will follow. We remark that regular languages and context free languages (which we will discuss in
this part of the course) have additional interesting applications that we will only mention.
2. The Turing Machine model of computation and decidable languages: In the second part of the course
we will introduce (arguably) the most important computational model known as Turing machine, and
study the class of languages that it computes. We will argue that this model captures anything that can
be computed by modern computers (at least in theory), and among other things, we will prove that
there are tasks that cannot be computed altogether.
3. Complexity theory: In the third and final part of the course we will introduce several efficiency mea-
sures of Turing machines, and discuss the question of what efficient Turing machines/algorithms can
compute. We will define the classes P, NP and the theory of NP-completeness.
For example, we will discuss the traveling salesman problem (TSP problem), which is defined by a weighted
graph G = (V, E). You should think of V as a list of cities, and on the weight of an edge e = (a, b) ∈E as
the cost to move from city a to city b. The problem is to find the cheapest tour that visits all the cities.

Definition 1.7. A language L ⊆Σ∗is called regular if there exists a DFA M that accepts it, i.e., such that
L(M) = L.
By definition, the languages that the DFAs M1, . . . , M5 accept are all regular. However, for the language
L2 we did not manage to construct a DFA, so we do not know if it is regular or not. Indeed, we stress that the
fact that we did not manage to construct a DFA does not mean there is no DFA! Over the next few lectures
we will study regular languages and develop tools that will help us to show that a given language is regular,
as well as tools that help us to show that a given language is not regular.
